Unlike traditional terrain-matching approaches, ROOKIE also considers critical differences between Earth and the Moon, including vacuum, reduced gravity, dust, and experimental scale. Our vision includes small-scale vacuum-chamber testing to evaluate sensors and subsystems under controlled conditions.

Our future ROOKIE SCOUT robot will collect real-time field measurements to validate predictions and improve site selection.

Because we can't bring the Moon to Earth, but ROOKIE can help us prepare for it.
details:
ROOKIE — Guiding Lunar Exploration, One Test at a Time

Every great mission needs a guide.

Rookie is not just the name of our project. He is a real guide dog being trained by Marom, one of our team members, to help people who are blind navigate the world safely and independently.

A guide dog learns to recognize obstacles, understand unfamiliar environments, and guide people toward safer paths.

That inspired us to ask a question:

What if we could build a guide dog for lunar exploration?

A system that helps engineers navigate the enormous challenges of preparing spacecraft to land on the Moon.

That's how ROOKIE was born.

The Challenge

Landing on the Moon is one of the most demanding engineering challenges in space exploration.

Before a lunar lander reaches the surface, engineers must prepare it to operate under extreme conditions: unfamiliar terrain, unpredictable surface properties, reduced gravity, lunar dust, extreme temperatures, and near-vacuum.

But Earth is fundamentally different from the Moon.

Testing a landing system in the wrong terrestrial environment can produce misleading results, while reproducing every lunar condition in a laboratory is expensive and technically challenging.

We believe that the first step toward safer lunar exploration is asking a deceptively simple question:

Where on Earth should we test our lunar technology?

Our Solution — Meet ROOKIE

ROOKIE is an intelligent platform designed to discover terrestrial testing locations tailored to the specific engineering requirements of lunar missions.

Instead of limiting engineers to a predefined list of familiar lunar-analog sites, ROOKIE aims to discover promising new locations by analyzing geographic datasets and comparing relevant surface characteristics.

The process begins when an engineer selects a lunar destination and defines the experiment they want to conduct.

ROOKIE then considers the experiment's physical requirements, available terrain measurements, geographic constraints, and environmental limitations.

Its discovery engine searches available Earth datasets for candidate testing regions.

Rather than overwhelming engineers with raw measurements, ROOKIE presents actionable information:

WHERE to test.

WHY that location is promising.

WHAT still needs to be measured.

HOW to validate the experiment.

Our goal is to turn complex scientific data into clear engineering decisions.

Beyond Terrain — The Importance of Vacuum

One of the most important aspects of ROOKIE is recognizing that finding terrain similar to the Moon is not enough.

The Moon has an extremely low-pressure environment, and vacuum can fundamentally change how certain physical systems behave.

For example, the behavior of rocket exhaust interacting with lunar dust differs significantly from the behavior observed under Earth's atmospheric conditions.

That's why ROOKIE is designed to consider vacuum requirements as part of the experiment-planning process.

Our vision includes combining terrestrial field experiments with small-scale laboratory vacuum testing.

Engineers could test selected subsystems, sensors, electronics, or representative physical interactions inside controlled vacuum chambers, while using reduced-scale experimental setups to investigate relevant operating conditions.

These experiments could help engineers evaluate sensor performance, system responses, thermal behavior, and computational workloads under carefully defined test scenarios.

Crucially, ROOKIE would distinguish between what can be validated through outdoor terrain testing and what requires a dedicated vacuum chamber or additional physical simulation.

Reduced-scale testing would also require appropriate scaling laws and engineering validation. A small vacuum chamber cannot automatically reproduce lunar gravity or every aspect of the lunar environment.

Our objective is not simply to find Moon-like terrain, but to help engineers design experiments that provide meaningful evidence about lunar performance.

Meet ROOKIE SCOUT — Our Future Robotic Explorer

Our long-term vision goes beyond software.

We envision ROOKIE SCOUT, a robotic field explorer that travels to candidate testing sites and collects real-world engineering measurements.

Equipped with suitable sensors and modular instruments, the robot could investigate terrain geometry, obstacles, surface characteristics, and selected geotechnical properties.

ROOKIE SCOUT could collect measurements during field experiments, transmit results to the platform, and help engineers compare predicted conditions with actual observations.

In the future, these measurements could improve the platform's models and support more informed site selection.

This creates a continuous learning process:

DISCOVER → MEASURE → VALIDATE → LEARN

The robotic system is a future development concept, while our current prototype focuses on the digital discovery and experiment-planning platform.

Our Technology

We developed ROOKIE using Python, geospatial data-processing methods, terrain-analysis algorithms, and interactive web technologies.

The current prototype incorporates:

  • Lunar mission and experiment configuration.
  • Geographic processing and terrain-feature extraction.
  • Candidate discovery using available Earth elevation data.
  • Interactive lunar and terrestrial visualizations.
  • Experiment-specific evidence and data-quality reporting.
  • Environmental testing considerations, including vacuum and reduced gravity.

Our development also incorporates NASA-related lunar and terrestrial data requirements, with additional data-provider integrations planned.

The current system uses limited real terrestrial elevation coverage and synthetic lunar data for parts of the prototype. Global discovery, fully validated lunar comparisons, and scientifically approved site rankings remain future development milestones.

We designed the system to distinguish measured evidence from missing information rather than present unsupported conclusions.

What Makes ROOKIE Different?

ROOKIE is designed around a principle:

The best testing location is not necessarily the place that looks most like the Moon. It is the place that provides the most relevant evidence for a specific engineering experiment.

Our approach combines three capabilities:

Intelligent Discovery: Finding geographic candidates through data analysis rather than relying only on known analog sites.

Physics-Aware Experiment Planning: Considering terrain, scale, environmental conditions, and the limitations of terrestrial testing.

Future Physical Validation: Connecting software predictions to real measurements from field instruments, robotic systems, and controlled laboratory experiments.

Over time, this approach could create a valuable database connecting satellite observations, physical terrain measurements, and experimental outcomes.

Our Vision

We want to make lunar engineering testing more accessible, efficient, and scientifically informed.

By helping teams identify promising testing locations, understand environmental limitations, and plan meaningful validation experiments, ROOKIE aims to reduce uncertainty before expensive lunar missions are launched.

And just like the real Rookie learns to guide people safely through unfamiliar environments, our platform aims to help engineers navigate the unknowns of lunar exploration.

We can't bring the Moon to Earth—but ROOKIE can help us discover where and how to prepare for it.

ROOKIE — Discover on Earth. Prepare for the Moon.
